title: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
story_key: story|title:clawdos an ai coding agent for dos
content_excerpt: An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS. Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API. title: Aletheia Aegis: Deterministic sub-millisecond output guard for AI agents
story_key: story|title:aletheia aegis deterministic sub millisecond output guard for ai agents
content_excerpt: Sub-millisecond runtime enforcement and output safety for autonomous AI agents. Fail-closed on credentials & life-safety. A deterministic, sub-millisecond guard for model outputs. Fail-closed on irreversible harm, fast enough to sit on every response, with an optional semantic judge for the cases patterns cannot settle. Aegis is the output plane of the Aletheia safety framework. It inspects generated text before it reaches a user, blocks credential leaks and life-safety failures outright, and flags everything else for audit or disclaimer. It runs offline by default, on CPU, with no response text retained. Built for platform, security, and AI infrastructure teams deploying tool-using agents into regulated or high-throughput production environments. Production agents need safety that does not break the product. The common approach, running a second LLM as judge on 100 percent of outbound traffic, fails on three counts at scale: Aegis takes the opposite starting point: enforce the non-negotiable invariants deterministically, at wire speed, and reserve model judgment for the small set of cases where semantics actually matter. That is the core design bet. Deterministic first, semantic second, fail-closed throughout. Stage 1: Deterministic edge engine. Every output is evaluated on CPU in 0.019 to 0.029 ms at p95. Irreversible failures trigger an immediate hard block. The upstream judge is skipped entirely, which saves cost and removes the exfiltration path. Stage 2: Optional semantic judge. For subjective or complex epistemic checks, an external judge (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini) can be called under strict rubrics. Detected secrets are masked before dispatch, life-safety findings can never be overruled, and heuristic defenses catch reviewer-targeted prompt injections. Aletheia standardizes nine failure signatures across the agentic lifecycle, grounded in 2,571 real-world incident records from the AI Incident Database, AVID, and the MIT AI Risk Repository. Aegis covers the output plane. Its companion, aletheia-mcp, covers the action plane. S3 is split by plane by design, so no single layer is a single point of failure: Benchmarked on Linux x86_64 and Apple Silicon, Node.js 18/20/22, single core unless noted. Held-out evaluation used 575 real model outputs across 30+ open and frontier models. Batches 10-11 replay offline with no external API cost: Labels were committed before measurement. The 90.2 percent figure is the balanced-policy result with the semantic judge

title: NPM package installed Hermes Agent as root and tasked it over Telegram
story_key: story|title:npm package installed hermes agent as root and tasked it over telegram
content_excerpt: The malicious npm package @leadstack/crm-connect installed a full AI agent on the servers it reached. It posed as the official client for a CRM called LeadStack. On install it set up Hermes Agent, an open-source agent from Nous Research that can run shell commands, edit files and drive a browser. It downloaded the agent’s keys and standing instructions from the attacker’s server and connected the agent to the attacker’s Telegram bot. Then it registered the agent as a systemd service renamed “LeadStack Lead Routing Daemon”. When npm install ran as root, the agent ran as root. From then on the attacker could give the server orders from a Telegram chat. The npm account zmaticoo published nine versions on 16 November 2026. SafeDep flagged the package five minutes after the last release, and npm has since removed it. In September, ThreatDown reported a botnet ⁠ (opens in new tab) that spreads through exposed Docker APIs and runs Hermes Agent as an implant. This is the first case SafeDep has seen of an npm install doing the same, with the agent’s persona downloaded at install time. The publisher is still active. Three packages it released on 18 November contain no code of their own and pull a dependency from the attacker’s server instead. The npm user zmaticoo (venstate25@gmail[.]com) published all nine versions between 09:44 and 15:27 UTC. The package described itself as “Official LeadStack CRM client”. Its early READMEs asked for “LeadStack partner access on npm (private org)”, and every version except the last set "access": "restricted" in publishConfig . The npmmirror copy, which still serves every tarball, records the package as created at 15:26 UTC, a minute before the last release. That suggests the package stayed private for most of the day. Only npm can confirm it. Version numbers 1.0.0 to 1.0.14, 1.0.16, 1.0.17 and 1.0.22 to 1.0.28 do not appear on the mirror. The payload moves to the first SDK call, then to a module downloaded from the server. LeadStack is a borrowed name. The package’s docs point at api.leadstack.io , a host that does not resolve. The domain leadstack.io belongs to an unrelated business consultancy that has nothing to do with this package. Version 1.0.15 carries the agent install in full. title: How Public Evals Work and Fail, and What Should Change
summary: How to read eval scores and what to question, from a teardown of 12 benchmarks.
story_key: story|title:how public evals work and fail and what should change
content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
story_key: model:claude code|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
summary: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

title: From Cases to Criteria: Reusing Evaluation Knowledge for Task-Specific Rubric Generation
summary: Query-specific rubrics make LLM evaluation more fine-grained and transparent, and generating high-quality rubrics requires both identifying the target query's evaluation scope and specifying concrete checks. Historical rubrics provide reusable evaluation experiences, yet existing approaches reuse either complete query-rubric cases or aggregated criteria and dimensions without explicitly connecting recurring evaluation requirements to their criterion-level evidence and source-query context. This can preserve irrelevant task details or lose the broader evaluation structure. In this paper, we introduce RubricDuo, which organizes historical query-rubric pairs into a Rubric Knowledge Graph linking evaluation dimensions, shared concepts, local concepts, criteria, and queries, where reusable evaluation requirements across queries are abstracted by shared concepts. Given a target query, RubricDuo first combines concepts relevant to the target query with retrieved historical cases to draft a rubric with broad coverage. It then revisits each draft criterion, retrieves concept-linked historical criteria and their source queries, and adapts applicable evidence to refine the criterion. Experiments on RubricBench and HealthBench demonstrate that RubricDuo achieves the overall best performance among the evaluated automatic methods in both alignment with human-authored rubrics and downstream LLM judging.

title: BADAS-3.0: Real-Time Driving Perception and Planning from One Camera
summary: We ask how far a driving model can get with one camera and real-time latency. BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads. From two seconds of one forward camera, it predicts the current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, BADAS-3.0 has 44% lower minADE$_6$ over five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, which reads six cameras and runs over 100x slower. The gain comes from camera rigs that neither model was trained on. On the rig they share, the two are on par. Existing benchmarks are mostly nominal driving, so we add two open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of Euro NCAP scenarios. On both, BADAS-3.0 has a higher pass rate than every published planner we tested.

title: Why agent governance starts with observability
summary: A strong AI agent governance strategy
story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective.   • Fixed a new skills, commands or agents folder being missed when --add-dir names the working directory or Claude Code starts in the home folder
  • Fixed sessions started from a pre-warmed process ignoring the autoCompactWindow setting in the project's .claude/settings.json
  • Fixed CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE staying in effect in a running session after it is removed from settings.json
  • Fixed the Agent tool's effort parameter being ignored for named teammates in agent teams
  • Fixed /auto-mode-setup ignoring recent auto mode denials when it scans a project for rules to suggest; it may now offer allow rules from them, and you review each before it's saved
  • Fixed a false "Couldn't save this change" warning after adding a permission rule or directory in a subfolder or worktree whose own .claude/settings.local.json is unreadable or malformed
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude to run a network proxy check after a failed request, which auto mode then blocked
  • Fixed headless rewind and fork going ahead while a message sent right after a model change still waited on it
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a background task was stopped while a cloud session was restarting
  • Fixed /team-onboarding reporting a guide as shared on Team and Enterprise plans when the server refused the upload
  • Fixed panels and questions being cut off at the prompt in fullscreen, /help, history search and the background tasks list losing rows or titles in short windows, and tables wrapping in dialogs
  • Fixed resumed sessions showing "Rejected" or "Declined" for edits, questions and plans that were cut off when the session ended
  • Fixed /passes showing the wrong number of passes after a server error, and offering usage credits for sharing when no guest passes are left
  • Fixed claude --help output being cut short when piped to another program
  • Fixed /terminal-setup turning on "Use Option as Meta key" in Terminal.app on macOS 27, and tips there suggesting Option+Enter instead of Shift+Enter
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed setup failing on Git LFS repositories cloned through Anthropic-managed git; sessions now start on pointer files, and git lfs pull fetches the content
  • Fixed sessions on self-hosted environments not starting from a git remote with an SSH host alias, GitHub SSH certificates or a GHE.com SSH user; an unresolved alias's error gives two git commands
  • Fixed remote MCP servers in self-hosted runner sessions staying without tools, or (over https) disconnected, after a timeout or network error
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as having stopped responding while Claude Code was still starting
  • Fixed Code Mode keeping in memory every large text file that code read, and memory growing each time a background subagent was woken
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script at its ten-minute limit while an MCP form, an MCP link prompt or a prompt that always asks was waiting for an answer
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts receiving a "moved to the background" message as data from most MCP calls over two minutes: the script now waits up to ten minutes, then gets an error
  • Fixed mods that list only some tools silently turning Code Mode off; such a mod no longer keeps it off, so use managed settings for that
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn when the tool was called from a script that Claude waits for
  • Fixed a Code Mode script's let x; keeping the value that an earlier script gave x
  • Fixed a Code Mode script's call with no argument failing with a missing-parameter error on tools that need none
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts losing access to tools through tools in sessions with more than 4,096 tools
  • Fixed the /code-review findings card often showing "high" for a review that ran at medium, on most models
  • Fixed key hints in permission prompts, questions, /model and /rewind ignoring keybindings.json
  • Fixed auto-scroll, the PR status badge, the auto-compact warning and the ultracode tag not following the /config switches that control them in a running session
  • Fixed a custom cancel key not working in /add-dir, /tui feedback and the save-workflow form
  • Fixed arrow keys in the save-workflow form moving the selection in the workflow view behind it
  • Fixed /config saying nothing, or "dismissed", after changing many settings
  • Fixed Read and @-mentions showing one line too many for files that end in a newline
  • Fixed /status not naming the model that opusplan and haiku use in plan mode
  • Fixed claude doctor advising a Keychain unlock inside a macOS sandbox, where unlocking can't help
  • Fixed the "Jump to bottom" pill staying hidden after copying text and scrolling away, the row under it going blank when its label changed, and quick PageUp presses scrolling too far in fullscreen
  • Fixed a screen update sometimes being skipped when memory is low
  • Fixed long code blocks losing a blank line and repeating another in scrollback
  • Fixed prompt suggestions sometimes showing placeholder text such as _(no suggestion)_
  • Fixed the line about earlier messages on resume blaming a damaged file when the file was intact
  • Fixed characters disappearing from the prompt when its text held a color code that sets several styles and a keyword or command was highlighted
  • Fixed /rename and UserPromptSubmit hook titles in claude remote-control sessions not showing on claude.ai and mobile
  • Fixed the Remote Control diff listing a file twice when the branch renamed it and it was then edited
  • Improved the automatic clean-up of old sessions on computers with managed settings
  • Improved /tui and other in-place restarts to wait briefly for a login refresh, so they are less likely to sign you out
  • Improved memory use in long sessions that edit many files, and in long Claude Desktop sessions on macOS and Linux with many large MCP tool results
  • Windows: Improved start-up and the first search on PCs where Claude Code's search program starts slowly
  • Improved auto mode's handling of a short reply such as "yes" to Claude's question when telemetry is off, behind a gateway to the Anthropic API, or on Microsoft Foundry
  • Improved memory use of idle Claude Desktop and SDK sessions after a long turn, and after --resume or --continue of a session that holds screenshots or large tool results
  • Improved how fast a Claude Desktop Code session with Remote Control on is ready for the next message after an answer
  • Improved cloud sessions to retry plugins that failed to download at startup
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Improved Code Mode: after starting a subagent, Claude now gets the same guidance on waiting as outside Code Mode
  • Updated computer use on macOS to newer safety rules, so some actions are refused and some apps have less access
  • Changed saved scheduled tasks: in new signed-in sessions, most saved by earlier versions need scheduling again, though --resume of their own session still runs them
  • Changed /code-review with no target on most models to review the whole branch against the default branch, and fixed it losing the diff on multi-commit branches
  • Changed auto mode to run git status less often so most requests wait less in large repositories; a git command that discards changes may be blocked until the working tree is checked
  • Changed /code-review <pr number> --fix, and /code-review given a pull request URL, to stop without reviewing when gh pr diff is refused or fails
  • Changed 'Exit and stop tasks' to end this session's scheduled tasks so they don't run again on resume, unless you exit while Claude is responding
  • Changed some teammate panes to start through /bin/sh, so they may not read shell start-up files
  • Changed computer use on macOS to give up on an app launch that has not finished after 30 seconds
  • Gateway: Changed the start-up warning shown while access_control.allow_cidrs is empty to a notice at every start, boxed in text logs: never expose the gateway to the public internet
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a second host name's clone of the same owner/name to go under _repos/clones/<host>/ in the base folder; no clone moves
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed repositories with unusual characters in their address path to clone anew in a new folder; rules and volumes naming the old one stop applying, and the old clone stays put
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed --repository-folder to take most folders in the base folder at --capacity 1 (above 1, one there stops start-up); another repository's session overlapping one is refused
  • Changed Code Mode so a PreToolUse hook that errors no longer refuses a script's tool call, as outside Code Mode; set "onFailure": "block" on a command, HTTP or MCP tool hook that must refuse
  • Changed Code Mode to refuse a script's read of a line range over 256 MiB, which could use gigabytes of memory, and fixed reads of very long lines timing out
  • Changed Code Mode to also start when telemetry, nonessential traffic or feature flags are turned off; an administrator can keep it off in managed settings
  • Changed Code Mode to run a script that declares its own log, preview or sleep, which it used to refuse
  • Changed macOS login renewal to test the Keychain with a Claude Code-write-check item
  • Changed the /tasks header and the footer's background count to one number covering shells, monitors, MCP calls, agents, workflows and scheduled tasks
  • Changed Stop and SubagentStop hooks to list a Monitor's script as monitor, not shell, in background_tasks
  • Removed 2.1.326's automatic retry at the limit named in a max_tokens error; behind a gateway whose model takes fewer output tokens, set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS to that limit
  • [VSCode] Added a line above the message box after you decline the trust prompt, with Review trust to bring the prompt back without reloading the window
  • [VSCode] Fixed being signed out of Claude Code in every window and terminal when the sign-in server took 10 to 30 seconds to answer the extension's token refresh
  • [VSCode] Fixed keys pressed while an input method (IME) is composing moving focus on or declining a permission prompt, running menu rows and closing dialogs (#106358)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for Bash, Edit, Write and other built-in tools not showing why a safety check asks
  • [VSCode] Fixed a half-written plan comment being lost or moved to another passage, and an input method's Enter sending the comment, ending a session rename or picking an @-mentioned file
  • [VSCode] Fixed the limit banner not saying when usage credits are in use, and the session survey covering that banner and the usage credits card
  • [VSCode] Fixed screen readers not announcing a permission request that arrived while the Account & Usage dialog was open until that dialog was closed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a proposed-edit diff tab staying open, with an Accept button that did nothing, after its terminal Claude Code session disconnected
  • [VSCode] Fixed short tool inputs and outputs cut off at the panel's edge with no way to read the rest (they now open in an editor tab), and dragging to select text also opening one
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Up key putting an earlier message over text that an input method (IME) is composing in the message box (#101294)
  • [VSCode] Fixed dropping an Explorer folder onto the chat inserting nothing on VS Code 1.103 to 1.139 or in a floating chat window, and the drop highlight vanishing with a false "Hold Shift" hint
  • [VSCode] Fixed a permission prompt moving keyboard focus away from the details you were scrolling as its buttons switched on
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening in another editor group when claudeCode.lockEditorGroups is off (#108884)
  • [VSCode] Fixed ranges written with a single tilde (3~5 … 7~10) losing their tildes and showing struck-through text between them; only ~~text~~ is struck through now
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation errors wrapping into a narrow column, the spinner turning while a question card waits, and a NUL symbol after each letter in the output of a failed UTF-16 command
  • [VSCode] Changed Down to stop at the last item of a permission prompt instead of wrapping to Yes
  • [VSCode] Changed command output to show hidden characters and control sequences other than plain colors as symbols, so Persian, Khmer, Lao, Sinhala and Malayalam text can look broken or out of order

title: Genie 4 is now available
story_key: story|title:genie 4 is now available
content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. title: Paul Stack: I'll Never Write Infrastructure as Code Again
summary:
Paul Stack helped build Terraform. Now he says he'll never write another line of infrastructure as code, because an agent harness runs his team's production infrastructure instead.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/kpo

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Guy Podjarny sits down with Paul, who spent years on Terraform at HashiCorp and on Pulumi before Swamp, to unpack why agents still trip over infrastructure state, what it takes to run a software factory that automates software delivery all the way to production, and why the people who know the system still make the calls. Then stay for Paul's full DevCon talk, From Page to Dossier, on a lights-out factory that does the 3am on-call legwork before anyone is woken up.

What we cover:
– Why agents still struggle with infrastructure as code, and why state is the hard part
– Model problem or harness problem: what an agent harness for operations needs
– Running an AI-first software factory from issue to production
– Blast radius, deterministic workflows and keeping credentials away from agents
– Why agents love toil, and why operators still own the judgment
– Paul's AI DevCon talk: turning a 3am page into a ready-made dossier

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction
00:02:21 - From Terraform and Pulumi to Swamp
00:04:19 - How good are agents at infrastructure as code?
00:07:28 - Model problem or agent harness problem?
00:09:54 - Do we still need infrastructure as code?
00:12:53 - Inside an AI-first software factory
00:15:34 - Blast radius, determinism and agent credentials
00:18:48 - Agents love toil: the ops harness engineer
00:21:49 - Why software factories need ops
00:27:35 - AI DevCon talk: From Page to Dossier

Book early for AI DevCon London 2027, 7–8 June at The Brewery, Moorgate:
https://tessl.co/wzi

🔔 Subscribe for weekly episodes on AI-native development

Would you trust an agent harness to run your production infrastructure, or does your team still want a human on every apply? Tell us in the comments.
